messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
For the forward direction, if M is complete and (F_n) satisfies the hypotheses, one can choose x_n in F_n, and then for m>n one has d(x_n,x_m) ≤ diameter(F_n), so (x_n) is Cauchy, it converges to some x, and closedness of each F_k gives x in every F_k, hence in their intersection.
For the reverse direction, if the nested-closed-set condition holds and (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence, one can choose increasing integers N_n such that d(x_i,x_j)<2^{-n} whenever i and j are at least N_n, one can define F_n to be the closure of the set of terms x_i with i at least N_n, and one can note that because a closure does not increase diameter these F_n are nonempty, closed, nested, and have diameters at most 2^{-n}, so their intersection contains some x, and for i at least N_n both x_i and x lie in F_n, forcing d(x_i,x)≤2^{-n} and therefore showing x_n converges to x.
Would you like the Cauchy-sequence construction expanded into a standard epsilon proof?
